screens.title: Achieving High Availability with EC2 and Auto Scaling
screens.narratorSegment: High availability begins by removing single points of failure. In AWS that means distributing compute across multiple Availability Zones, placing a load balancer in front to route traffic, and using Auto Scaling Groups to automate recovery and elasticity. In this chapter you will learn what Multi-AZ deployments protect you from, how an ASG performs self-healing and capacity management, and why pairing an ELB with ELB-based health checks produces a robust system. We will use concrete examples like a simple web application running Apache across two AZs, a launch template with user data to bootstrap servers, and an ALB target group combined with an ASG that uses ELB health checks. You will also see common mistakes, such as relying only on instance-level status checks or using overly heavy health probes. By the end, you should be able to design and validate an EC2 architecture that stays online when an AZ fails, scales with demand, and replaces unhealthy instances automatically. Consider how your application responds when one data center becomes unavailable — this chapter gives you the practical tools to prevent downtime.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to design EC2 architectures that resist single AZ failures, configure Auto Scaling Groups to maintain desired capacity and replace unhealthy instances, integrate an Elastic Load Balancer to distribute incoming requests across AZs, and design health checks that measure application readiness rather than just instance availability. Each objective links a practical skill to a reason it matters. For example, deploying across multiple Availability Zones matters because a single data center failure should not bring your service offline. Configuring an ASG matters because it automates recovery and keeps capacity stable during planned maintenance or unplanned failures. Using an ALB matters because it allows content-based routing and health-aware traffic distribution. And building robust health checks matters because a bad check can either hide failures or cause unnecessary instance replacement. These are the competencies you'll verify with a hands-on activity and an assessment question that asks you to choose the best pattern to survive an AZ loss.

screens.title: Multi-AZ Deployments
screens.narratorSegment: Multi-AZ deployment means placing your compute resources in more than one Availability Zone within the same AWS Region. An Availability Zone is an independent failure domain — one or more data centers with separate power, networking, and connectivity. The central claim is simple: a single EC2 instance or a single AZ can fail, and your application should still serve users. For example, deploy two Apache web servers in two different AZs. If one AZ becomes unreachable, the load balancer routes traffic to the other AZ where healthy instances continue serving requests. A common misconception is that distributing instances across subnets alone is sufficient; the real benefit comes from spreading instances across AZs physically separated by independent infrastructure. This protects you from power or network failures limited to one AZ. When you design for Multi-AZ, also ensure your supporting resources like databases and storage are replicated or accessible across AZs. A thoughtful takeaway: Multi-AZ reduces the blast radius of an outage, but it does not replace the need for health checks and auto-replacement of failed instances. How would you verify that your service stays responsive if one AZ fails? Plan a test where you simulate instance failure and observe traffic rerouting and capacity adjustments.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Multi-AZ Deployments
Multi-AZ Deployment
Distribute EC2 instances across independent Availability Zones to avoid a single point of failure.
Definition: AZs are isolated failure domains; multi-AZ means at least two AZs per tier.
Example: Two Apache servers in AZ-A and AZ-B, with an ALB routing traffic to both.
Misconception: Subnets alone do not guarantee AZ separation; verify the AZ property of each subnet.
Key Takeaway

Place instances in multiple AZs to reduce outage impact; combine this with load balancing and ASG for resilience.

Scenario
E-commerce website: deploy two EC2 instances in separate AZs so a data center failure won't drop the storefront.
Verification steps
  1. Confirm instance AZs in the EC2 console or with CLI describe-instances.
  2. Ensure there are active targets in more than one AZ for your load balancer.
  3. Simulate a failure and watch traffic shift to the healthy AZ.

screens.title: Auto Scaling Groups (ASG)
screens.narratorSegment: An Auto Scaling Group is a logical collection of EC2 instances that you manage as a single unit. The ASG maintains a desired capacity: a minimum, maximum, and target number of instances. Its two most important roles are elasticity and self-healing. Elasticity means the group can scale out or in based on demand or scheduled policies so your application has enough capacity. Self-healing means the ASG monitors instance health and replaces instances that fail health checks, restoring capacity without manual intervention. For example, if you set desired capacity to two and one instance crashes, the ASG will launch a replacement to return to two instances. A typical mistake is setting overly wide min/max values or relying only on manual monitoring. Another mistake is failing to tie the ASG to an ELB health check; by using ELB health results, the ASG can act on application-level failures rather than just instance-level status. Remember to configure a health-check grace period so instances have time to boot and register. The practical outcome: ASGs let you define intent — how many instances you want — and AWS enforces that intent automatically. Reflect on what desired capacity should be during maintenance windows and how scaling policies affect user experience.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Auto Scaling Groups
Auto Scaling Groups
Define min, max, and desired capacity and let the ASG manage instance lifecycle automatically.
Desired capacity: the target number of instances the ASG works to maintain.
Self-healing: ASG can terminate unhealthy instances and launch replacements.
Scaling: Use policies based on CPU, request count, or schedules to adjust capacity.
Common mistake

Relying only on EC2 status checks or not using ELB health checks can leave application failures undetected. Use application-level checks where possible.

Example flow
1. ASG desired capacity = 2
2. Instance fails application health check
3. ASG terminates unhealthy instance
4. ASG launches new instance to restore capacity
Key Takeaway

ASGs express intent for capacity and automate recovery. Configure health checks and grace periods to avoid false replacements.

screens.title: Launch Templates and User Data
screens.narratorSegment: A launch template stores the configuration needed to create EC2 instances, including AMI, instance type, security groups, and user data. User data is a script that runs at first boot and is essential for installing software and configuring the instance to serve traffic. For example, use user data to install Apache, start the web server, and write a basic index page. This ensures new instances launched by an ASG are ready to accept traffic after they pass health checks. A common mistake is placing heavy initialization tasks in the health path or not allowing enough time for initialization. Use a health-check grace period to give user-data scripts time to complete before the ASG starts evaluating health. Below is the sample user data from the chapter that installs httpd and writes a simple page. Note that this code runs during instance launch; do not place long-running database migrations here unless you use background techniques. Bootstrapping reduces manual configuration and speeds recovery when the ASG launches replacements. Launch Templates and User Data means use launch templates with concise user data to make instances ready and avoid blocking health checks during initialization.. In practical terms, bootstrapping ec2 instances so they serve traffic immediately. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Launch Templates
Launch Template + User Data
Store instance configuration and a small boot script to install and start your service at launch.
Why it matters: Bootstrapped instances become productive immediately, enabling faster replacement by ASG.
Misconception: Avoid long-running tasks in user data that delay health checks and block scaling.
Set a health-check grace period so your user data can finish before health evaluation begins.
User data example
#!/bin/bash
yum update -y
yum install -y httpd
systemctl start httpd
systemctl enable httpd
echo "<h1>Hello from my Highly Available Web Server!</h1>" > /var/www/html/index.html
This script installs and starts Apache then writes a simple index page. Keep scripts idempotent and lightweight.

screens.title: Elastic Load Balancing: ALB, NLB, GLB
screens.narratorSegment: Elastic Load Balancing includes several types of load balancers, each optimized for different needs. The Application Load Balancer, or ALB, is designed for HTTP and HTTPS traffic and provides Layer 7 features like path or host-based routing. Use an ALB when you need content-aware routing, such as directing A P I traffic to one set of instances and web traffic to another. The Network Load Balancer, or NLB, operates at Layer 4 and excels at ultra-low latency and handling millions of connections; it is useful for TCP, UDP, or TLS where raw performance and static IPs are required. The Gateway Load Balancer helps deploy third-party virtual network appliances and scales them transparently. A common misconception is choosing NLB for all performance reasons; if you need request-level routing or host header rules, ALB is usually the right choice. For our e-commerce example, an ALB is appropriate because it handles HTTP and provides health checks and target groups. Always match the ELB type to protocol and routing needs, then register the ASG's instances with the appropriate target group for correct health monitoring and traffic distribution.

keyIdea.text: Choose ALB for HTTP/HTTPS and routing, NLB for extreme performance and static IPs, GLB for third-party appliances.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Elastic Load Balancing
Application Load Balancer (ALB)
Best for HTTP/HTTPS, content-based routing, host and path rules, and metrics at request level.
Use when you need Layer 7 features and application-aware routing.
Network Load Balancer (NLB)
Best for millions of requests, very low latency, TCP/UDP/TLS protocols, and static IP requirements.
Use when raw performance and static IP addresses matter more than request routing.
Gateway Load Balancer (GLB)
Designed to deploy and scale third-party virtual appliances like firewalls and intrusion detection systems.
Use when you need a transparent gateway for virtual network appliances.
Example decision
For a web application serving HTTP content across AZs, choose ALB to leverage path-based routing and ALB health checks. Register the ASG targets in the ALB target group so the ASG can use ELB health checks if configured.

screens.title: Target Groups and ELB Integration
screens.narratorSegment: Target groups are a logical grouping of endpoints, such as EC2 instances, that a load balancer routes traffic to. When you create an ALB you create one or more target groups and register instances or IPs as targets. The ELB polls targets and uses health check results to decide where to send requests. Integrating the ASG with the ELB means you attach the ASG to an ALB target group so new instances are registered automatically when launched. This integration is important because the ASG can be configured to use ELB health checks; when the ELB marks a target unhealthy, the ASG can terminate that instance and launch a new one to maintain capacity. A common trap is registering instances manually with a load balancer while an ASG also manages the fleet; prefer attaching an ASG to a target group so registration and de-registration happen automatically. In practice, ensure your target group health check path is lightweight and specific to application readiness. Think about how the target group will distribute traffic across AZs and what thresholds will balance sensitivity to failures against false positives.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Target Groups
Target Groups & ELB
A target group collects endpoints and exposes a health check that the load balancer uses to route traffic to healthy targets only.
  • Registration: ASGs attached to a target group register instances automatically when they launch.
  • Health driven: ALB marks unhealthy targets and stops sending traffic to them.
  • ASG integration: If ASG uses ELB health checks, an unhealthy target can be terminated and replaced.
Example configuration
Create a target group for HTTP on port 80, set health check path to /status or /index.html, and attach the ASG to this target group. Ensure the ASG's VPC subnets span multiple AZs so targets appear in each AZ.
Key Takeaway

Use target groups as the integration point between ELB and ASG to enable automatic registration and health-aware replacement of instances.

screens.title: Health Checks: ELB vs ASG
screens.narratorSegment: Health checks are the mechanism that tells both the load balancer and the Auto Scaling Group whether an instance is fit to receive traffic. The ELB periodically probes targets with an HTTP request or a TCP probe. If a target fails its health checks, the ELB marks it unhealthy and stops sending traffic. ASGs perform instance status checks by default, but they can be configured to use ELB health checks instead. Using ELB health checks is stronger because the load balancer is aware of application-level readiness. For instance, an EC2 instance might pass system status checks but the web server may be hung; an HTTP health check to a /health endpoint catches that. A typical flow: ALB health probe fails → ELB marks target unhealthy → if ASG uses ELB health checks, ASG terminates the instance → ASG launches replacement to maintain desired capacity. Common mistakes include using health checks that are too heavy, causing performance impact, or thresholds that are too aggressive, causing unnecessary replacements. Design a health endpoint that is quick, safe, and representative of application readiness, and tune thresholds and grace periods to match boot and warm-up behavior.

keyIdea.text: ELB health checks detect application-level failures; configuring ASG to use ELB checks enables true self-healing of unhealthy instances.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Health Checks
ELB and ASG Health Checks
Health checks are the linking mechanism for traffic routing and instance lifecycle management.
  • ELB checks: HTTP GET or TCP probes to validate target readiness.
  • ASG checks: EC2 status checks by default, but can use ELB results for app-level decisions.
  • Flow: ELB marks unhealthy → ASG replaces instance if configured to use ELB checks.
Best practices
  1. Use an application endpoint like /health that checks runtime dependencies.
  2. Keep checks lightweight to avoid added load or security issues.
  3. Tune health thresholds and grace period to avoid false positives during boot.
Common Mistake

Checking only instance running state or probing heavy operations can hide real failures or cause unnecessary churn. Prefer a quick, representative endpoint.

screens.title: Hands-on: Create ALB, Launch Template, and ASG
screens.narratorSegment: This guided activity walks you through creating an Application Load Balancer, a launch template with user data, and an Auto Scaling Group attached to a target group. Start by creating the ALB and choosing two public subnets in different AZs so your load balancer is multi-AZ. Create a target group for HTTP on port 80 and set the health check path to a lightweight page such as /index. html. Next, create a launch template using an Amazon Linux AMI, a small instance type, the appropriate security group allowing HTTP and SSH, and include user data that installs and starts Apache and writes an index page. Finally, create an Auto Scaling Group using that launch template, attach it to your target group, and set desired capacity to two with a max of four. Configure health-check-type to ELB and a sensible grace period. After creation, verify the ALB DNS name returns your page and then terminate one instance to observe the ASG replacing it. This demonstrates the full loop: ALB routes traffic, health checks detect failure, and ASG restores capacity. Hands-on: Create ALB, Launch Template, and ASG means build the alb, launch template, and asg; attach target group and verify self-healing by terminating an instance.. In practical terms, a stepwise plan to build a highly available web application and verify self-healing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Hands-on Activity
Activity steps
  1. Create an Application Load Balancer across at least two public subnets in different AZs.
  2. Create a target group for HTTP:80 and set health check path to /index.html.
  3. Create a launch template with user data to install and start Apache.
  4. Create an Auto Scaling Group, attach it to the target group, and set health-check-type to ELB.
  5. Verify the ALB DNS returns the index page, then terminate one instance to watch ASG replace it.
CLI snippet (create ASG)
# Create Auto Scaling Group using existing launch template and target group
aws autoscaling create-auto-scaling-group \
  --auto-scaling-group-name MyWebServerASG \
  --launch-template LaunchTemplateName=MyWebServerLaunchTemplate,Version='$Latest' \
  --min-size 2 \
  --max-size 5 \
  --desired-capacity 2 \
  --vpc-zone-identifier "subnet-0abcdef...,subnet-0fedcba..." \
  --health-check-type ELB \
  --health-check-grace-period 300 \
  --target-group-arns "arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:...:targetgroup/MyTargetGroup/..."
This command shows how the ASG uses a launch template, spans subnets, and relies on ELB health checks to maintain desired capacity.

screens.title: E-commerce Example Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Consider an e-commerce application serving storefront traffic. The architecture uses an Application Load Balancer fronting an Auto Scaling Group of EC2 instances spread across at least two Availability Zones. The ALB has a target group with HTTP health checks to a simple /status or /index. html endpoint. The launch template installs Apache, starts it, and provides the page used by the health check. The ASG is configured with desired capacity of two and a max of four; it is attached to the ALB's target group and set to use ELB health checks. If a server becomes unresponsive to HTTP probes, the ALB marks it unhealthy and stops sending traffic. Because the ASG uses ELB health checks, the ASG will terminate the unhealthy instance and launch a replacement. This preserves desired capacity and ensures that user requests continue to be served by healthy instances. A common nuance: ensure that database or shared state is also available across AZs or externalized, because booting replacement instances only handles compute failures, not data availability issues. The core learning point: the combination of ALB routing, application-level health checks, and ASG enforcement yields a resilient, self-healing service.

screens.title: Tuning Health Checks and Grace Periods
screens.narratorSegment: Health checks must be tuned so they are sensitive to real failures but not so aggressive that they cause unnecessary instance churn. Start by making the health endpoint lightweight and deterministic. For web servers, an HTTP GET to /health or /index. html that verifies service dependencies is better than a deep integration test. Next, set sensible thresholds for healthy/unhealthy counts and intervals so transient spikes or slow boots don't cause immediate replacement. Use a health-check grace period on the ASG to give new instances time to finish user data and register with the load balancer. For example, if your user data installs packages and configures the app in two minutes, a grace period of 300 seconds prevents premature termination. A common error is using a heavy check that queries databases on every probe, which increases load and can mask real problems. Another is setting thresholds too strict — too many consecutive failures before marking unhealthy can delay replacement. The practical step: observe boot and warm-up times in your environment and set intervals and counts so checks reflect steady-state readiness rather than temporary delays.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Tuning Health Checks
Design health checks
Keep checks quick, representative, and safe. Avoid heavy operations that add load or risk security exposure.
Lightweight endpoint: /health that confirms basic dependencies.
Grace period: Allow user data to finish before health evaluation.
Thresholds: Set consecutive success/failure counts to avoid flapping.
Example
If boot takes around 120 seconds for your AMI, set a health-check grace period of 300 seconds. Use health-check interval and unhealthy thresholds that tolerate brief network hiccups.
Quick checklist

  • Observe real boot times and tune grace period accordingly.
  • Avoid checks that perform heavy database queries on every probe.

fullNarratorScript:
High availability begins by removing single points of failure. In AWS that means distributing compute across multiple Availability Zones, placing a load balancer in front to route traffic, and using Auto Scaling Groups to automate recovery and elasticity. In this chapter you will learn what Multi-AZ deployments protect you from, how an ASG performs self-healing and capacity management, and why pairing an ELB with ELB-based health checks produces a robust system. We will use concrete examples like a simple web application running Apache across two AZs, a launch template with user data to bootstrap servers, and an ALB target group combined with an ASG that uses ELB health checks. You will also see common mistakes, such as relying only on instance-level status checks or using overly heavy health probes. By the end, you should be able to design and validate an EC2 architecture that stays online when an AZ fails, scales with demand, and replaces unhealthy instances automatically. Consider how your application responds when one data center becomes unavailable — this chapter gives you the practical tools to prevent downtime.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to design EC2 architectures that resist single AZ failures, configure Auto Scaling Groups to maintain desired capacity and replace unhealthy instances, integrate an Elastic Load Balancer to distribute incoming requests across AZs, and design health checks that measure application readiness rather than just instance availability. Each objective links a practical skill to a reason it matters. For example, deploying across multiple Availability Zones matters because a single data center failure should not bring your service offline. Configuring an ASG matters because it automates recovery and keeps capacity stable during planned maintenance or unplanned failures. Using an ALB matters because it allows content-based routing and health-aware traffic distribution. And building robust health checks matters because a bad check can either hide failures or cause unnecessary instance replacement. These are the competencies you'll verify with a hands-on activity and an assessment question that asks you to choose the best pattern to survive an AZ loss.

These objectives are the practical checks you will perform in the hands-on activity. You will verify that instances launch in multiple AZs and remain reachable through an Application Load Balancer. You will confirm an Auto Scaling Group replaces an unhealthy instance automatically when ELB marks it unhealthy. You will demonstrate a launch template with user data that installs a web server, and you will test an ALB health endpoint to ensure it accurately reflects application readiness. Each objective links a real action to its operational value. For example, testing the ALB's health endpoint verifies that the load balancer sends traffic only to instances that are serving the application, not just to instances that have booted. These verifications demonstrate the resilience patterns described earlier and prepare you to tune health checks and scaling policies for production workloads.

Multi-AZ deployment means placing your compute resources in more than one Availability Zone within the same AWS Region. An Availability Zone is an independent failure domain — one or more data centers with separate power, networking, and connectivity. The central claim is simple: a single EC2 instance or a single AZ can fail, and your application should still serve users. For example, deploy two Apache web servers in two different AZs. If one AZ becomes unreachable, the load balancer routes traffic to the other AZ where healthy instances continue serving requests. A common misconception is that distributing instances across subnets alone is sufficient; the real benefit comes from spreading instances across AZs physically separated by independent infrastructure. This protects you from power or network failures limited to one AZ. When you design for Multi-AZ, also ensure your supporting resources like databases and storage are replicated or accessible across AZs. A thoughtful takeaway: Multi-AZ reduces the blast radius of an outage, but it does not replace the need for health checks and auto-replacement of failed instances. How would you verify that your service stays responsive if one AZ fails? Plan a test where you simulate instance failure and observe traffic rerouting and capacity adjustments.

An Auto Scaling Group is a logical collection of EC2 instances that you manage as a single unit. The ASG maintains a desired capacity: a minimum, maximum, and target number of instances. Its two most important roles are elasticity and self-healing. Elasticity means the group can scale out or in based on demand or scheduled policies so your application has enough capacity. Self-healing means the ASG monitors instance health and replaces instances that fail health checks, restoring capacity without manual intervention. For example, if you set desired capacity to two and one instance crashes, the ASG will launch a replacement to return to two instances. A typical mistake is setting overly wide min/max values or relying only on manual monitoring. Another mistake is failing to tie the ASG to an ELB health check; by using ELB health results, the ASG can act on application-level failures rather than just instance-level status. Remember to configure a health-check grace period so instances have time to boot and register. The practical outcome: ASGs let you define intent — how many instances you want — and AWS enforces that intent automatically. Reflect on what desired capacity should be during maintenance windows and how scaling policies affect user experience.

A launch template stores the configuration needed to create EC2 instances, including AMI, instance type, security groups, and user data. User data is a script that runs at first boot and is essential for installing software and configuring the instance to serve traffic. For example, use user data to install Apache, start the web server, and write a basic index page. This ensures new instances launched by an ASG are ready to accept traffic after they pass health checks. A common mistake is placing heavy initialization tasks in the health path or not allowing enough time for initialization. Use a health-check grace period to give user-data scripts time to complete before the ASG starts evaluating health. Below is the sample user data from the chapter that installs httpd and writes a simple page. Note that this code runs during instance launch; do not place long-running database migrations here unless you use background techniques. Bootstrapping reduces manual configuration and speeds recovery when the ASG launches replacements. Launch Templates and User Data means use launch templates with concise user data to make instances ready and avoid blocking health checks during initialization.. In practical terms, bootstrapping ec2 instances so they serve traffic immediately. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Elastic Load Balancing includes several types of load balancers, each optimized for different needs. The Application Load Balancer, or ALB, is designed for HTTP and HTTPS traffic and provides Layer 7 features like path or host-based routing. Use an ALB when you need content-aware routing, such as directing A P I traffic to one set of instances and web traffic to another. The Network Load Balancer, or NLB, operates at Layer 4 and excels at ultra-low latency and handling millions of connections; it is useful for TCP, UDP, or TLS where raw performance and static IPs are required. The Gateway Load Balancer helps deploy third-party virtual network appliances and scales them transparently. A common misconception is choosing NLB for all performance reasons; if you need request-level routing or host header rules, ALB is usually the right choice. For our e-commerce example, an ALB is appropriate because it handles HTTP and provides health checks and target groups. Always match the ELB type to protocol and routing needs, then register the ASG's instances with the appropriate target group for correct health monitoring and traffic distribution.

Target groups are a logical grouping of endpoints, such as EC2 instances, that a load balancer routes traffic to. When you create an ALB you create one or more target groups and register instances or IPs as targets. The ELB polls targets and uses health check results to decide where to send requests. Integrating the ASG with the ELB means you attach the ASG to an ALB target group so new instances are registered automatically when launched. This integration is important because the ASG can be configured to use ELB health checks; when the ELB marks a target unhealthy, the ASG can terminate that instance and launch a new one to maintain capacity. A common trap is registering instances manually with a load balancer while an ASG also manages the fleet; prefer attaching an ASG to a target group so registration and de-registration happen automatically. In practice, ensure your target group health check path is lightweight and specific to application readiness. Think about how the target group will distribute traffic across AZs and what thresholds will balance sensitivity to failures against false positives.

Health checks are the mechanism that tells both the load balancer and the Auto Scaling Group whether an instance is fit to receive traffic. The ELB periodically probes targets with an HTTP request or a TCP probe. If a target fails its health checks, the ELB marks it unhealthy and stops sending traffic. ASGs perform instance status checks by default, but they can be configured to use ELB health checks instead. Using ELB health checks is stronger because the load balancer is aware of application-level readiness. For instance, an EC2 instance might pass system status checks but the web server may be hung; an HTTP health check to a /health endpoint catches that. A typical flow: ALB health probe fails → ELB marks target unhealthy → if ASG uses ELB health checks, ASG terminates the instance → ASG launches replacement to maintain desired capacity. Common mistakes include using health checks that are too heavy, causing performance impact, or thresholds that are too aggressive, causing unnecessary replacements. Design a health endpoint that is quick, safe, and representative of application readiness, and tune thresholds and grace periods to match boot and warm-up behavior.
